reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: The most common complete vascular ring, in which both the right and left aortic arches persist and encircle the trachea and oesophagus.
The right (posterior) arch is dominant in the majority of cases, with the left arch smaller and occasionally atretic.
Symptoms arise from tracheo-oesophageal compression, including biphasic or expiratory stridor, a barking cough, recurrent respiratory infection and feeding difficulty with dysphagia.
Reflex apnoea or so-called dying spells, sometimes precipitated by feeding, can occur in infants.
CT or MR angiography defines the arch anatomy, the dominant arch and the airway compression, and is the mainstay of diagnosis.
A barium swallow classically shows bilateral indentations of the oesophagus with a prominent posterior compression.
Bronchoscopy demonstrates pulsatile external tracheal compression and helps assess associated tracheomalacia.
Treatment is surgical division of the ring, usually through division of the smaller (commonly left) arch, relieving the constriction around the airway and oesophagus.
reference.pathophysiology: A double aortic arch reflects failure of normal regression within the embryonic aortic arch system. Normally the right fourth arch and dorsal aorta regress distal to the right subclavian origin to leave a single left arch, but when both arches persist the ascending aorta divides into two limbs that pass on either side of the trachea and oesophagus and rejoin posteriorly to form the descending aorta. The two arches, together with the ligamentum arteriosum, create a complete ring that mechanically constricts the enclosed airway and oesophagus, and chronic pulsatile compression frequently produces secondary tracheomalacia.
additionalDifferentials: Right aortic arch with aberrant left subclavian artery and a left ligamentum (another complete ring)
additionalInvestigations: MR angiography as a radiation-free alternative
Transthoracic echocardiography for screening and associated cardiac lesions
Flexible or rigid bronchoscopy to assess airway compression and malacia
Chest radiograph noting the side of the aortic arch and tracheal deviation
Genetic testing including 22q11.2 microdeletion where indicated
redFlags: Acute life-threatening events or reflex apnoea during feeds
Severe stridor with respiratory distress or cyanosis
Failure to thrive from feeding-related airway compromise
Recurrent pneumonia suggesting significant airway obstruction
reference.prognosis: Surgical division is curative with low operative mortality and excellent long-term outcomes, although residual tracheomalacia may cause symptoms that resolve gradually over months to years.
pitfalls: Prolonged misdiagnosis as asthma, croup or reflux, delaying definitive imaging.
Relying on echocardiography alone, which may not fully delineate the ring or the airway.
Underestimating persistent tracheomalacia after division and expecting immediate symptom resolution.
Dividing the dominant rather than the smaller arch, compromising systemic perfusion.
Failing to identify an atretic segment that alters the surgical approach.
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
management: Surgical division of the vascular ring, dividing the non-dominant (usually minor left) arch together with the ligamentum arteriosum to free the encircled trachea and oesophagus, is the definitive and curative treatment
Reserve early operation for infants with stridor, recurrent respiratory infection, feeding difficulty or apnoeic spells, while a truly asymptomatic incidental ring may be observed
Provide supportive care with humidified respiratory support, prompt treatment of intercurrent chest infections and modified, unhurried feeding for dysphagia
Anticipate and manage persistent tracheomalacia after repair, which may need prolonged positive-pressure support and typically improves gradually over months to years
Recognise and urgently relieve reflex apnoea or acute airway obstruction (dying spells), which mandates expedited surgical decompression
Use bronchoscopic assessment of airway compression and malacia to guide timing of surgery and predict post-operative airway behaviour
Coordinate care across paediatric cardiology, cardiothoracic surgery, ENT and paediatric anaesthesia, with echocardiographic screening for associated cardiac lesions
